blocks.text: Propositional logic is a basic form of logic used in computer science. It deals with statements that can be true or false; these statements are called propositions (Fig 2.3).

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: Propositional logic is the simplest type of logic, but it forms the base of all computer reasoning.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.text: A proposition is a statement that is either true or false; it cannot be both at the same time.

Questions and commands are not propositions. For example, 'The sun rises in the east' is a proposition. A proposition must have a clear meaning and should not be confusing. Propositions are the basic units of logic and are used to form logical expressions. A proposition is usually represented by a capital letter such as P, Q or R; for example, P = 'The sky is blue'.

blocks.alt: Left panel, propositions: P: The sun rises in the east (value true); Q: 2 + 2 = 5 (value false); R: It is raining (true or false today); note: exactly one value, never both. Right panel, not propositions: Close the door (a command); What time is it? (a question); x is greater than 5 (depends on x, a predicate); note: no fixed true or false value.
blocks.caption: Propositions and sentences that are not propositions (original diagram after Fig 2.3).
blocks.long_description: The test for a proposition is simple: can you say it is true or false? A false statement is still a proposition; a question or command is not.

blocks.text: A simple proposition contains only one statement and cannot be broken into smaller parts, for example 'It is raining'. A compound proposition is formed by joining two or more simple propositions with logical connectives, for example 'It is raining and it is cold'. Compound propositions can express complex ideas and are common in logical reasoning.

Logical connectives join propositions. AND is true when both statements are true; OR is true when at least one statement is true; NOT reverses the truth of a statement (Fig 2.4). Connectives form compound propositions, are commonly used in computer programs, and help in decision making.

blocks.alt: Three Venn diagrams. A AND B: two overlapping circles with only the overlap shaded; true only if both are true. A OR B: both circles shaded; true if at least one is true. NOT A: everything outside circle A shaded; true if A is false.
blocks.caption: The logical connectives AND, OR and NOT (original diagram after Fig 2.4).
blocks.long_description: The shaded region shows where each expression is true. In symbols, AND is often written as an upward wedge, as in MCQ 6 of the exercise.
